Results of the sealed test evaluation

Three methods were frozen on training/validation data (commit 6240f60) and evaluated exactly once on two sealed test sets of 1,750 records each: test_iid (drawn like the training data) and test_shift (lower SNR, wider frequency range, more harmonics and unbalance, ±2 % calibration error and an unseen transient). Every number on this page comes from reports/results.json. All results are [SIM].

Headline

Macro-F1 averages the F1 score over the seven classes. ML methods: mean ± sd over three training seeds. False alarm = a normal record labelled as an event; miss = an event labelled normal.

Are the differences real?

Intervals: paired, class-stratified bootstrap 95 % confidence intervals of the macro-F1 difference (seed mean); McNemar: exact test on the records where exactly one of the two methods is right (per seed). "Better" is claimed only if the CI excludes zero.

Where performance drops: SNR

Severity and the unseen transient (test_shift)

The Blue Cut Fire check: a naive PLL frequency rule

A naive monitor flags a "frequency event" whenever its PLL frequency deviates by more than 1.0 Hz at any instant. That is how many inverters misread a phase jump in 2016. On the same test records:

The rules and GBM-embedded never confused a phase jump with a frequency event on either test set (critical confusion phase_jump↔freq_event: rules 0.0, GBM-embedded 0.0 on test_shift).

Model size versus validation F1

Every GBM-embedded grid configuration (largest size over 3 seeds) against its validation macro-F1. The selected model (13,972 bytes) is the smallest of the configurations tied at the top; GBM-unconstrained (~174,888 bytes equivalent) was the size-unbounded reference. Validation was saturated, so size could not buy robustness here.

Findings, in plain words

  1. On data like the training data, both are equally good. test_iid: GBM-embedded 1.0000 vs rules 0.9983; difference +0.0017, 95 % CI [+0.0000, +0.0040] — no significant difference.
  2. Under shift the rules are significantly better. test_shift: rules 0.9902, GBM-embedded 0.8653 (difference −0.1250, CI [−0.1407, −0.1101]). From iid to shift the rules lose −0.008, the tree model −0.135. When noise and nuisances leave the training range, the learned model degrades sharply; the rules barely move.
  3. Where the model fails: phase jumps and false alarms at low SNR. GBM-embedded (seed 0) on test_shift recognised only 38 % of phase jumps (107 called normal, 38 oscillation) and flagged 56 normal records (53 as oscillation). Seed mean: 23.3 % false alarms, 7.3 % misses. The model learned noise-dependent shortcuts; the physical jump threshold does not depend on noise.
  4. A bigger model did not help. GBM-unconstrained: test_iid 1.0000, test_shift 0.8484 with 58.1 % false alarms.
  5. Safety-critical confusions stay at zero for the rules and GBM-embedded (phase jump vs frequency event, sag vs normal), while the naive PLL rule flags 100 % of phase jumps as frequency events.
  6. The rules' errors come from the measurement chain. The rules made 17 errors on test_shift (3 on test_iid), 13 of them phase jumps whose half-cycle RMS crossed 0.90/1.10 transiently; the others come from calibration error and the unseen transient. Fixed IEC thresholds are robust to noise but sensitive to calibration — which is why the C2000 integration makes calibration mandatory.
  7. Embedded cost does not decide. The tree model adds about 239 comparisons and 13,972 bytes of flash to a 1,517,143-operation feature pipeline that both methods share. Robustness decides.

Limitations

  • Synthetic data from this project's own generator: training, validation and both test sets share its physics; the shift is one designed nuisance configuration. The rules were written by people who know the generator.
  • Strong-grid assumption; no converter or PCS dynamics; single-label records with label margins (no multi-event or threshold-straddling records).
  • No measured data (no [EXP] evidence); timings are from a PC.
  • Validation was saturated (many GBM configurations tied at the top), so model selection could not prefer robust models; the GBM was trained without noise augmentation.

What would change the conclusion

  • A GBM trained on shift-like conditions (wider SNR and calibration ranges) that then matches the rules on new shift-like data: the finding would become "ML needs representative training conditions".
  • Restricting the model to physically motivated features or monotonic constraints.
  • Measured PCS records with real noise, converter dynamics, calibration drift and multi-event cases — the rules' fixed thresholds could fail there too.
  • A confidence-gated hybrid (use the model only when it is confident, otherwise the rules), evaluated on new sealed data (the current test sets are no longer blind).
